c.tagline: Mediterranean island capital of light and cathedrals.

emergency.note: 091 (national police), 092 (local police) and 061 (health emergencies) also work; 112 operators handle English.

hood_landmark.Casco Antiguo (Old Town): La Seu, Palma's landmark Gothic cathedral
hood_landmark.Santa Catalina: the Mercat de Santa Catalina food market and its tapas bars
hood_landmark.El Terreno: circular hilltop Bellver Castle overlooking the bay
hood_landmark.Portixol: the old fishing port's marina and seafront promenade
hood_landmark.Playa de Palma: The long sand beach and its numbered balneario beach bars

avoid.reason: The Son Gotleu estate and neighboring working-class blocks east of the center see gang-related trouble and hold nothing for tourists.
Pickpockets work the Playa de Palma strip, La Lonja's nightlife lanes and the airport bus, with bag snatching a risk late at night.

hood_desc: Casco Antiguo (Old Town) is Palmas historic heart, a maze of medieval lanes, Gothic cathedral views, boutiques and tapas bars; ideal for first-time visitors and culture lovers who want to walk everywhere.

Santa Catalina is a hip, foodie district built around a lively market, packed with trendy restaurants, cocktail bars and cafes; suits younger travelers and food enthusiasts wanting buzz within walking distance of the center.

El Terreno is a hillside neighborhood below Bellver Castle with sea views and a faded bohemian, nightlife past; appeals to budget-minded travelers who want proximity to the port and a quieter, slightly gritty local feel.

Portixol is a charming former fishing village on the seafront with a scenic promenade, sandy beach and stylish brunch spots; perfect for couples and design-conscious travelers seeking a relaxed coastal base near the city.

Playa de Palma is the city's long resort beach strip, running from the marina at Ca'n Pastilla through Les Meravelles towards s'Arenal: several kilometres of sand backed by a dense wall of package hotels, beach bars and a seafront cycle path, roughly 10 km east of the old town and linked to it by bus. It suits beach and nightlife holidays rather than sightseeing.
lodging: AC Hotel by Marriott Ciutat de Palma

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many prefer bottled due to a mineral/desalinated taste.

transit.pay: Pay with the islandwide TIB intermodal smartcard or, on EMT city buses, simply tap a contactless bank card, Apple Pay or Google Pay when boarding. A single EMT bus ride is €2 in cash (about $2.30) but only around €1.20 (~$1.40) by contactless card; tickets and cards are also sold at EMT and TIB kiosks, station machines, and on board.
transit.hours: EMT buses run from about 5:30-6am to around 11pm-midnight depending on route; the M1 metro line runs roughly 6:30am-10pm weekdays (shorter Saturdays, no Sunday service), with no regular overnight service.
transit.note: Transit really only covers Palma city and a short metro line, so exploring the rest of Mallorca's beaches, villages and the Serra de Tramuntana mountains usually needs a rental car, taxi or rideshare.

transit.m: Airport bus A1 to Placa Espanya, 25 min

food.name: Ensaimada
food.desc: Coiled, feather-light pastry made with lard and dusted in icing sugar; plain, or filled with pumpkin jam, cream or sobrassada.

places.name: Ca'n Joan de S'Aigo
places.note: Trading since 1700, all marble tables and chandeliers; ensaimada with thick hot chocolate.

places.name: Fornet de la Soca
places.note: Revivalist bakery using local organic flour and old Mallorcan recipes.

places.name: Forn Fondo
places.note: Long-standing bakery on Carrer Unio turning out classic boxed ensaimadas to take home.

food.name: Sobrassada
food.desc: Soft, spreadable cured pork sausage deep red with paprika, eaten on bread, warmed with honey, or stirred through island cooking.

places.name: Mercat de l'Olivar
places.note: The city's main market, best place to compare artisan sobrassada and island cheeses.

places.name: Colmado Santo Domingo
places.note: Narrow shop hung floor to ceiling with sausages; buy vacuum-packed to travel.

places.name: Mercat de Santa Catalina
places.note: Smaller local market with charcuterie stalls and bars that serve it on toast.

food.name: Tumbet
food.desc: Layered bake of fried potato, aubergine and red pepper under a slow-cooked tomato sauce - Mallorca's summer vegetable classic.

places.name: Celler Sa Premsa
places.note: Cavernous 1958 cellar lined with wine barrels; no bookings, so arrive at opening.

places.name: Ca'n Carlos
places.note: Small family restaurant that has cooked strictly Mallorcan dishes for decades.

places.name: Bar Espana
places.note: Long-running tapas bar doing a homely tumbet alongside island staples.

food.name: Frit mallorqui
food.desc: Rustic fry-up of potato, peppers, fennel and offal or fish, sharpened with garlic and bay. Hearty, cheap and thoroughly local.

places.name: Celler Sa Premsa
places.note: One of the few central places still serving the full traditional version.

places.name: Ca'n Carlos
places.note: Well-regarded kitchen for old island recipes rarely seen on tourist menus.

places.name: Mercat de l'Olivar
places.note: Market bars upstairs cook a lunchtime frit for market traders and locals.

food.name: Arros brut
food.desc: Soupy dark rice with rabbit, pork, mushrooms and island spices - the 'dirty rice' that Mallorcan families cook in cooler months.

places.name: Celler Sa Premsa
places.note: Big portions of the classic version at old-fashioned cellar prices.

places.name: Ca'n Carlos
places.note: Slow-cooked and richly spiced; worth booking as the dining room is tiny.

places.name: Mercat Gastronomic Sant Joan
places.note: Food hall in an old slaughterhouse with several Mallorcan-cooking stalls.

food.name: Pa amb oli
food.desc: Dense brown bread rubbed with ramallet tomato and olive oil, topped with cured ham, sobrassada or Mahon cheese. The island's default snack.

places.name: Bar Rita
places.note: Little square-side bar much loved for its pa amb oli boards and low prices.

places.name: La Rosa Vermuteria
places.note: Vermouth bar with good bread, island charcuterie and a bustling early-evening crowd.

places.name: Mercat de Santa Catalina
places.note: Buy the ingredients at the stalls or eat it made-to-order at the market bars.

food.name: Hierbas mallorquinas
food.desc: Anise liqueur steeped with rosemary, fennel and lemon leaves. Comes dry, sweet or mixed, and is served ice-cold after a meal.

places.name: Celler Sa Premsa
places.note: A chilled shot after the arros brut is practically part of the house ritual.

places.name: Bar Rita
places.note: Friendly place to try the dry version without ceremony or markup.

places.name: La Rosa Vermuteria
places.note: Good spot to compare seques and dolces styles side by side.

food.name: Binissalem and Pla i Llevant wines
food.desc: Mallorca's own denominations, built on the native Manto Negro and Callet reds and Prensal Blanc whites - rarely exported, so drink them here.

places.name: Vinostrum
places.note: Wine shop and bar on Carrer Sant Feliu with a deep Mallorcan by-the-glass list.

places.name: Wineing
places.note: Self-serve wine machines let you taste small pours of many island bottles.

places.name: Mercat de l'Olivar
places.note: Buy a bottle from the market wine stall and drink it at the tapas counters.

landmarks: Palma Cathedral (La Seu)
A monumental Gothic cathedral rising dramatically over the seafront, widely considered Mallorca's most photographed landmark.
Royal Palace of La Almudaina
A former Moorish alcazar turned royal palace beside the cathedral, blending Islamic and Gothic architecture.
Bellver Castle
A rare circular Gothic castle on a hilltop overlooking Palma Bay, offering panoramic views of the city and sea.
Plaça Major
A grand arcaded 18th-century square in the old town, lively with cafes, artists, and market stalls.
Passeig del Born
An elegant tree-lined boulevard connecting the old town to the harbor, historic Palma's central promenade.
Basílica de Sant Francesc
A striking 13th-century basilica with a beautiful Gothic cloister, tucked into the old city's winding streets.
Arab Baths (Banys Àrabs)
One of the few remaining relics of Moorish Palma, a small horseshoe-arched bathhouse set in a lush garden.
Palma Marina & Seafront
A scenic harbor lined with yachts and palm trees, with the cathedral as a dramatic backdrop across the bay.
Es Baluard Museum
A contemporary art museum built into a 16th-century bastion wall, combining modern architecture with sea views.
Santa Catalina Market & Neighborhood
A trendy former fishing quarter with a historic covered market, colorful facades, and a lively food scene.

train.note: Mallorca is an island, so there are no international or mainland trains. SFM runs the local rail lines from Palma's Intermodal station to Inca, Sa Pobla and Manacor plus the Palma metro. The historic Ferrocarril de Soller scenic train is run separately (https://trendesoller.com/en/).

bus.note: No international or mainland coach routes exist from an island. The islandwide TIB bus network (https://www.tib.org/en/) links Palma with the rest of Mallorca.

ferry.note: There are no international ferries from Palma. Balearia (https://www.balearia.com/en) and Trasmed (https://www.trasmed.com/en/) sail from the Estacio Maritima to mainland Spain (Barcelona, Valencia, Denia) and the neighbouring Balearic islands - all domestic Spanish routes.

half.name: Sóller
half.blurb: People ride the vintage wooden train through orange groves to this charming mountain valley town.

half.name: Valldemossa
half.blurb: A postcard stone village in the hills known for its monastery where Chopin once stayed.

half.name: Deià
half.blurb: An artists' village clinging to the mountainside above the sea, long a haven for writers.

half.name: Cuevas del Drach
half.blurb: Visitors descend into dramatic caves with an underground lake and live classical music concerts.

half.name: Alcúdia
half.blurb: A medieval walled town with Roman ruins, a lively market and long sandy beaches nearby.

half.name: Pollença
half.blurb: People climb the 365 Calvari steps and browse the Sunday market in this laid-back old town.
